solutions.title: Leave the last move forced
solutions.explanation:
Every allowed move sends each corner to an adjacent corner. This sharply restricts the possible configurations after an odd number of moves.

Split the corner positions into the two opposite pairs
\[
\{(1,1),(-1,-1)\},\qquad \{(-1,1),(1,-1)\}.
\]
Each move switches these pairs. Thus, after \(19\) moves, vertex \(A\) must occupy either \((-1,1)\) or \((1,-1)\).

For either position of \(A\), there are only two neighboring positions for \(B\). Rotations and reflections preserve adjacency and opposite vertices, so \(C\) must be opposite \(A\), and \(D\) must be opposite \(B\). Therefore there are at most \(2\cdot2=4\) possible complete configurations after \(19\) moves.

The single moves \(L,R,H,V\) produce four distinct configurations of this kind. Indeed, rotations preserve the cyclic direction of the labels while reflections reverse it, and within each type the two moves put \(A\) in different positions. These four configurations therefore exhaust the possibilities after \(19\) moves.

Consequently, every nineteen-move sequence has the same overall effect as exactly one allowed move. Its inverse is also allowed: \(L\) and \(R\) undo each other, while \(H\) and \(V\) each undo themselves. Exactly one final move restores all four labels.

We may choose the first \(19\) moves freely, with four choices each, and then the last move is forced. Different prefixes give different full sequences, and every successful sequence has such a prefix. Hence the number is
\[
4^{19}=\boxed{2^{38}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Count two moves at a time
solutions.explanation:
Two consecutive moves have only four possible overall effects. Grouping the twenty moves into ten pairs lets us count these effects recursively.

Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(x,y)&=(x,y),&T(x,y)&=(-x,-y),\\
F(x,y)&=(y,x),&G(x,y)&=(-y,-x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(I\) does nothing, \(T\) is a half-turn, and \(F,G\) are reflections across the diagonals.

The following table gives every ordered pair of allowed moves, applying the row move first and the column move second.

| First move | Then \(L\) | Then \(R\) | Then \(H\) | Then \(V\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(L\) | \(T\) | \(I\) | \(G\) | \(F\) |
| \(R\) | \(I\) | \(T\) | \(F\) | \(G\) |
| \(H\) | \(F\) | \(G\) | \(I\) | \(T\) |
| \(V\) | \(G\) | \(F\) | \(T\) | \(I\) |

For example, \(L\) followed by \(H\) sends
\[
(x,y)\longmapsto(-y,x)\longmapsto(-y,-x),
\]
which is \(G\). Each of the four effects appears exactly four times in the table.

These effects remain within the same set under composition: each either swaps the coordinates, negates both, does both, or does neither. Swapping and negating both commute, and repeating either operation undoes it. Moreover, from any fixed current effect, the four possible pair effects give four distinct resulting effects, since the current effect is invertible. Thus exactly four choices of the next ordered pair lead to each target effect.

After one pair, there are \(N_1=4\) sequences ending at each effect. If there are \(N_j\) sequences per effect after \(j\) pairs, each of the four current effects contributes \(4N_j\) sequences to a fixed target. Therefore
\[
N_{j+1}=16N_j.
\]
After ten pairs, the number ending at \(I\) is
\[
N_{10}=4\cdot16^9=\boxed{2^{38}}.
\]
Each twenty-move sequence has a unique division into these consecutive pairs, so the count has no omissions or repetitions. The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
